entries.title: About the Course
entries.content:
Read about Canadian history from 1800-1900 through books that immerse students in the time period and allow them to see the world through the eyes of those who lived it. Through engaging narratives, biographies, history spines, primary source documents, oral histories, historical fiction, and books that show different perspectives, students come to see history as more than dates and events and develop relationships with people from the past. Viewing images, looking at maps, and working on one's Book of Centuries are also part of developing this relationship.

This topic is included in the following course(s): History: Grades 7-8 (Canada)

entries.title: Placement & Combining Tips
entries.content: Canadian history may be suitable for grade 9 students if combining.

blocks.text:
• Read through the lesson and gather any necessary links. 

• If you have not read the book, you may want to read the selected pages in advance. 

• Decide which lessons/books to read together and which to have students read independently.

• Connect back to the previous lesson. Have students give a summary of what they remember. (Full narration is not necessary.)

• If the previous passage is difficult to remember, teachers may ask a leading question: "What can you tell me about..." Or students may try looking back at any chapter/section headings or illustrations or reading the first paragraph to jog the memory.

• Use a picture, map, or engaging question to pique the student's interest in the day's lesson (often included in lesson plans). 

• If necessary, talk about a few unfamiliar words that will be crucial to understanding.

• Read the day's passage out loud or have the student read independently. Sometimes reading for the specified time is a better guide.

• If a book is challenging, try stopping to narrate every now and then rather than waiting until the end. It can also help to read aloud. Or you might want to use an audiobook version of the text and have students read along with it.

• Have students keep an eye out for events or characters to add to their Citizenship Notebook, Book of Centuries, or Copywork Book.

• Have students retell the passage orally or write a narration. 

• Alternatively, students might analyze a character, trace cause to consequence, outline a passage, or use one of the other methods indicated by Charlotte Mason in School Education Chapter 16, especially p.180.

• Students who enjoy writing can experiment with different types of written narrations, but this is not required.

• Give the student an opportunity to share thoughts on the lesson and any connections made (orally or in writing). 

• You could ask them what they thought about the passage or ask an open-ended question to stimulate discussion. Discussion questions are often included in the lesson plans.
• Optional: Add something to the Book of Centuries, Century Chart, Citizenship Notebook, or Commonplace book. If students would like to include pictures, these may be drawn or printed.

lessons.title: 30m Canadian History: Grades 7-8 - Lesson 1
lessons.body:
Introduction - The War of 1812
⍞ Materials: Jeremy's War 1812

➜ INTRO
Throughout much of the eighteenth century and into the second decade of the nineteenth, the British Navy was engaged in near-continuous naval conflicts until peace was declared in 1815 after the Battle of Waterloo. One of Britain's last major battles before then was the War of 1812, in which Canada, then still a collection of British colonies, became the battleground for a conflict between the United States and Britain over many long-standing grievances, including shipping rights and American expansionist plans. 
The first historical novel we will read in this course is Jeremy's War 1812, a gripping account of the war told from the perspective of a fifteen-year-old orphaned boy who joins a regiment of British soldiers and eventually becomes the personal servant of Sir Isaac Brock. Historical details blend smoothly with a fictional story to create a detailed recreation of this definitive period in Canada's pre-Confederation history.

➜ VIEW
The following video gives some background on the stakes for Canada in the War of 1812 and its importance for Canada's history.
∞ Video Link: The War of 1812 | The Canadian Perspective 

➜ READ, NARRATE, & DISCUSS
p.7-18 "They were expecting me" - "and walked inside."
• Who are the characters you meet as the novel opens? How are they related to each other? What are they like? You may choose to keep a character list with some notes.

lessons.title: 30m Canadian History: Grades 7-8 - Lesson 2
lessons.body:
The War of 1812, cont.
⍞ Materials: Jeremy's War 1812

➜ RECAP
What did you learn about the characters of Jeremy and his uncle from the last reading?

➜ READ, NARRATE, & DISCUSS
p.19-32 "We were in a storeroom" - "continued down the road."
• What do you think of the choices Jeremy makes in this chapter? What would you have done in his place? What are you learning about his character, and what it was like to be a teenager in the nineteenth century?
lessons.teacherNotes:
★ TEACHER NOTE
Sensitive content, p.32: Parents and teachers may wish to explain that the word "rape" can also mean to snatch or take something by force; from the Latin rapio, which also gives us the English word 'raptor.'

lessons.title: 30m Canadian History: Grades 7-8 - Lesson 3
lessons.body:
The War of 1812, cont.
⍞ Materials: Jeremy's War 1812

➜ RECAP
Take a moment to recall Jeremy's situation at the end of the last reading.

➜ READ, NARRATE, & DISCUSS
p.33-46 "It was hard to sleep" - "have General Brock."
• Explain the causes of the War of 1812 as they are presented today's reading. What makes Captain Stanton hopeful for success?

➜ VIEW
Take a few minutes to look at this map of York, now Toronto, made in 1813. In today's reading, Jeremy travels south on Yonge St. (most likely the sole road on this map that stretches north through the forest). Notice in the "Remark" on the map, that bridges over the Don River to the east of York were "decaying fast" and "in so great danger of falling that it was thought requisite at this time (Nov 1813) to support." While the bridge that collapsed under Jeremy was north rather than east of York, this map shows that at this time bridges could be hazardous for travellers.
∞ Map Link: 1813 Sketch of York

lessons.title: 30m Canadian History: Grades 7-8 - Lesson 4
lessons.body:
The War of 1812, cont.
⍞ Materials: Jeremy's War 1812

➜ RECAP
What do you recall of Jeremy's introduction to the 41st regiment from the last reading? You may want to refer back to the 1813 map of York as you read about the regiment's march towards the the city.

➜ READ, NARRATE, & DISCUSS
p.46-58 "Brock. I'd heard the name" - "I wondered what he knew."
• What do you think of Jeremy's decision? What do you think life will be like for him in the army?

lessons.title: 30m Canadian History: Grades 7-8 - Lesson 5
lessons.body:
The War of 1812, cont.
⍞ Materials: Jeremy's War 1812

➜ RECAP
How did Jeremy describe the town of York and the garrison in the last reading?

➜ READ, NARRATE, & DISCUSS
p.59-71 "Mostly I remember" - "me to follow."
• What more do we learn about Jeremy's character from today's reading? How do you think he will fare as a batman? Why was he chosen?

➜ VIEW
Learn more through reenactments about the rations served to soldiers in the War of 1812 and the Brown Bess musket Jeremy learns to use in today's reading:
∞ Video Link: Food in the War of 1812 
∞ Video Link: The Brown Bess Musket in the War of 1812

lessons.title: 30m Canadian History: Grades 7-8 - Lesson 6
lessons.body:
The War of 1812, cont.
⍞ Materials: Jeremy's War 1812

➜ RECAP
What do you recall from the last reading?

➜ READ, NARRATE, & DISCUSS
p.71-83 "We were in a hallway" - "I kept my mouth shut."
• What are your first impressions of General Brock? Continue to add to your character list.

➜ VIEW
Over the course of the term, you will spend some time looking at the War of 1812 from four separate perspectives: the British, the Americans, the Canadians, and the Native Americans. Today, spend some time exploring the resources explaining the War of 1812 from the British perspective. Make some notes of what interests you.
∞ Link: The British War | 1812 Virtual Exhibition

lessons.title: 30m Canadian History: Grades 7-8 - Lesson 8
lessons.body:
The War of 1812, cont.
⍞ Materials: Jeremy's War 1812; map or atlas of Ontario

➜ RECAP
What do you recall about General Brock's plan from the last reading?

➜ READ, NARRATE, & DISCUSS
p.99-113 "We sailed through the night" - "if the Americans are eager to fight?"
• What did you learn in today's reading about some of the logistics and preparations required for a major battle? What were some of the obstacles to General Brock's preparations? Why did nearly a third of the new recruits need to be sent back to their farms?

➜ MAP WORK
Using a map or atlas of Ontario, locate Ancaster. Approximately how far a march would it have been from where the troops disembarked at Burlington Bay?

➜ VIEW
Today, spend some time exploring the resources explaining the War of 1812 from the American perspective. Make some notes of what interests you. Continue exploring these resources in future lessons.
∞ Link: The American War | 1812 Virtual Exhibition
lessons.teacherNotes:
★ TEACHER TIP
As you read today, continue to reference the map from the last lesson to plot the army's movement.

If you would like to map the major locations of the novel, you can do so on a blank map of the Great Lakes.
∞ Map Link: Blank Great Lakes Map

★ TEACHER NOTE
Sensitive content: there is a propaganda print illustrating the scalping of American soldiers under the "Getting into War" section that some students may wish to skip.
